title: Paul Fokam's Two-Year Wait for a Bank With No State Money
dek: In 1986 a Cameroonian economist won a presidential waiver to open a bank without public capital, then gave it a deliberately modest name.

story.company: Caisse commune d'épargne et d'investissement (later Afriland)
story.event: Winning a presidential waiver to license a Cameroonian bank with no public capital
story.summary: Paul Fokam first applied in 1984 to open a bank in Cameroon, where the law required at least 35 per cent public capital unless the president granted a waiver. After meeting President Paul Biya in September 1986 he obtained the waiver, and the licence was signed in November 1986. The bank, deliberately named Caisse commune d'épargne et d'investissement, opened its first branch in 1987 and later became Afriland First Bank.
paragraphs: In September 1986 Paul Fokam, a Cameroonian economist, obtained a meeting with President Paul Biya. He had worked for banks at home and abroad and had set up a small paper-products factory, Sitracel, and by his own account he had first applied to open a bank in 1984. The obstacle was a rule: unless the president granted a special waiver, a bank licence could go ahead only if public interests held at least 35 per cent of the capital. Fokam wanted a bank with no state money in it at all.

A waiver, he later wrote, needed reasons strong enough for the head of state to act on. One he points to lay in the law itself. Its explanatory memorandum, he says, had called for national interests in a bank's capital, not public ones; somewhere in turning it into the final text, national had become public. He gave a larger reason in a 2016 interview: the idea then current was that Africans could not run a bank, an airline or an insurer, and his project was designed to show that they could.

The meeting brought the waiver, and the licence was signed in November 1986. Fokam then chose a deliberately plain name: Caisse commune d'épargne et d'investissement, a common fund for savings and investment. He has given two reasons. He wanted the name itself to teach that saving feeds investment. And he expected officials of the day to resist a bank started by a compatriot with no state stake, so he decided to describe its purpose without announcing it.

The first branch opened in 1987, and in his telling the hard part began then. A technical adviser from the finance ministry arrived, Fokam says, with the job of stopping the bank before it could grow; years later the man told him he had missed his aim. The foundation that gave Fokam the German Africa Prize in 2005 describes the bank as the first, and at the time the only, commercial bank in Cameroon run by a Cameroonian, lending small sums to people other banks would not consider. Renamed Afriland First Bank, it grew into the country's largest locally owned bank, and Fokam went on to launch MC², a network of self-managed village microfinance mutuals that numbered 105 by 2015.

quote.text: Commend not a man for his beauty; and abhor not a man for his outward appearance. The bee is little among such as fly; and her fruit is the chief of sweetmeats.
quote.work: Ecclesiasticus (The Wisdom of Ben Sira) and the Wisdom of Solomon
quote.source_title: The Wisdom of the Apocrypha, Project Gutenberg eBook #77250
quote.connection: Fokam was answering a belief that Africans could not run banks, and he hid his bank's ambition inside a modest name. Ben Sira warns against judging by looks in either direction: the bee is small among flying things, and what it makes is the sweetest.

reflection: Two years passed between Fokam's first application and the signature. What he points to as moving it was a precise reason: a single word in the law that had changed between the draft and the final text. He also chose a name that would not provoke the people who could stop him, and kept his ambition for the work itself.

When you are waiting on someone else's approval, it is easy to spend the time pushing harder. Sometimes the better use is quieter: knowing the rule more exactly than the people applying it, and letting the rest of the wait be rest rather than worry.
invitation: Choose one approval or answer you are waiting for. Find the exact rule or document it depends on, read it through once today, and mark the single line that matters most.

cross_checks.claim: In September 1986 Fokam met President Biya to obtain a waiver from the rule requiring at least 35 per cent public capital in a bank, because he wanted a bank with no public money
The bank began as the Caisse commune d'épargne et d'investissement, opening in 1987, and later became Afriland First Bank
Fokam founded the bank in 1986-87 as a Cameroonian-run bank without state capital
Fokam later launched the MC² village microfinance network

research_notes: Dates: the Deutsche Afrika Stiftung gives 1986 as the founding year and Camer.be gives 1987; Fokam's own account (2020 book, quoted verbatim by EcoMatin) reconciles them: first application 1984, waiver after the September 1986 meeting with Biya, licence signed November 1986, first unit opened to customers in 1987. Profile sites not cited here (billionaires.africa, a student thesis on memoireonline) say the licence came in July 1987 with capital of 300 million CFA francs, and a branch directory says the first counter opened on 1 July 1988; none gives a primary source, so the story follows Fokam's account and does not state the capital. The slate framed the episode as 'years of rejection'; the sources document a two-year wait and a legal barrier, not repeated formal refusals, so the story says only that. The point about the explanatory memorandum ('national' becoming 'public' interests) and the finance ministry adviser sent to stop the bank are Fokam's own claims and are attributed to him; they have no independent confirmation. Fokam writes the abbreviation as CCEIB; other sources write CCEI; the story uses the full name. Doctorate timing conflicts (Jeune Afrique 2026 calls him a young doctor of management sciences in 1986; Jeune Afrique 2015 refers to his economics thesis of 1989), and his birthplace differs between sources (Camer.be: Boukué), so the story mentions neither. 'Largest locally owned bank' rests on EcoMatin's editorial (first Cameroonian-owned bank for a decade) and Jeune Afrique's description of Afriland as a banking giant; MC² claims of a million people helped are the network's own and are not used, only Jeune Afrique's count of 105 mutuals. All French passages are paraphrased in the writer's own translation; no French wording is presented as a direct English quotation. EcoMatin marks the page for subscribers but the full editorial and book extract are publicly visible; Jeune Afrique's 2026 portrait is paywalled after its first paragraph, and only that opening (September 1986 meeting, 35 per cent rule, no public money) is relied on. Not part of this episode, but reported elsewhere: Jeune Afrique's portrait mentions 'zones d'ombre', and the regional central bank has criticised the group's Geneva-based holding structure. Funding is marked unknown: the bank had no public capital, but the sources do not say who the first private shareholders were. Quote: Ecclesiasticus 11:2-3 as printed in the Wisdom of the East selection (1910), which follows the English Revised Version text; verses numbered from the chapter marker in the Gutenberg file.
